I notice in

Miners and Steel Workers
dangerous the situation is and how far it is possible to escape the conclusion that the Nova Scotia miners have come to regard the Nova Scotia government as being an agent in the hands of the British Empire Steel Corporation?

I saw in this
morning's paper the article to which my hon. friend refers, but I had not received any letter from Canon Scott at the time that I read it. I, however, thought it was important and I prepared an immediate reply. Just as I was leaving my office at five minutes to three o'clock, I was handed a letter, which I have in my hand at the moment, mailed at Quebec last night at ten p.m. It has Canon Scott's name on the envelope and I see from the contents it is signed by Canon Scott. I have not yet had an opportunity of reading the letter, but I have no doubt it is the same as the communication I read in the press. I will read to the House the reply which I gave to Canon Scott. Perhaps I should read first Canon Scott's letter to me. His letter reads as follows:
St. Matthew's Church
Quebec, March 24.
" Dear Sir:
" In the name of our country I appeal to you as the head of the federal government of Canada to take immediate steps to save the lives and stop the acute suffering of our 60,000 fellow citizens in Cape Breton.
" If there is no law in the constitution of Canada which gives you the right to avert the hideous calamity now very imminent the supreme law of common humanity empowers you to intervene.
" The funds of the relief committee, we are told by responsible people, including that of the Roman Catholic Bishop of Antigonish and the Anglican Archbishop of Halifax, are almost exhausted, and when they are gone, absolute starvation and death must ensue.
" Ultimately the responsibility of the fate of our fellow Canadians rests not upon one province only, but on the whole Dominion.	The ancestor whose name you so proudly bear, was once judged a rebel because he stood for the rights of the oppressed in defiance of the law. An oppressed people is crying for a deliverer to-day. Never in the whole course of our history has there been a more wonderful example of patient heroism than is being manifested by the thousands of men, women and little children in Cape Breton at the present time.
" If the agony of human beings does not move your government to immediate action, perhaps the reflection that failure to save the lives of Canadians now will not only shake your government, but, what is worse, it will shake the ordered constitution of our country.
" It is merely playing into the hands of that Bolshevism which we all dread, and which is threatening the governments of the world to-day. This should not be the motive to lead us to play fairly with our fellow Canadians, but it ought to have weight with those whose 6elf-interests shut their ears to the cry of the suffering.
" Yours faithfully,

To that communication I have sent the following reply:
Prime Minister's Office
Ottawa, March 25, 1925. Reverend Canon F. G. Scott, M.A., D.C.L.,
St. Matthew's Church,
Quebec, P.Q.
Reverend Sir,-I have read in this morning's paper an open letter, addressed by you to myself, the original of which has not yet been received. The letter constitutes an appeal on behalf of citizens in Cape Breton in need of relief.
Where in any emergency an appeal has been made by the government of any province of our Dominion on behalf of any of its citizens, the administration of which I have the honour to be the head has never failed to give such appeal careful and immediate consideration and to respond in the manner and to the extent circumstances appeared to warrant. I believe the provincial governments of our country have been equally ready to respond to appeals from municipalities within their jurisdiction where they were of the opinion that circumstances demanded such action in the name of their provinces.
Were it to be recognized that the government of Canada, without request from the government of the province concerned, more especially when its legislature is in session, upon appeal from a citizen of another province, thereby becomes obligated to use federal moneys of which it is the trustee to meet a purely local situation, however serious, I greatly fear the effect would soon be, if I may be permitted to quote the words of your letter, to " shake the ordered constitution of our country."
I share all your admiration for the patience of the men, women and children who have been called upon to endure privation and suffering in the present situation. I believe I am not less anxious than yourself to see existing distress speedily alleviated. I am equally cognizant of the fact that, as you intimate, our government may suffer politically through a misunderstanding of the motives which govern its action, should it hesitate to respond to your appeal. This, however, is not a circumstance which to my mind should influence the government in taking what appears to be the right and proper course in this matter.
The fact that federal moneys might, with the consent of parliament, be used towards relieving existing distress, possibly to the advantage of the government itself, does not free either my colleagues or myself from our responsibility of recommending to parliament a course of action which once adopted would open the door to inroads upon the federal treasury from every quarter of the Dominion, and which in the end might only serve to aggravate the present situation in Cape Breton and lead to similar conditions asserting themselves with increasing frequency wherever and whenever industrial troubles arise.
To avoid the very Bolshevism of which your letter makes mention, I feel that regard must be had by the federal government to what would appear to be the constitutional course of procedure in all matters which may involve rights and responsibilities on the part of municipalities, the governments of the several provinces and the government of the Dominion.
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.

I should like to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to a rule that prevents access to this chamber by members of the House unless the House is actually sitting. Why?
I do not think that is reasonable. I am at a loss to know what the idea is.

This is not the time to
bring up a question of this kind. I understand that there has been some trouble in connection with the main door in front, which is reserved for members of the House, for ministers of the crown, and for deputy ministers and secretaries. I have studied the rules of many of 'the parliaments in the empire and on the continent of Europe, and there is no legislative body in the world, so far as I know, in which access to the chamber is as easy as it is in the case of the Canadian parliament. I have visited the House of Commons in England myself, and before reaching the gallery I have been obliged to pass through several cordons of policemen and men-at-arms. And the same is true of the continent. The rule governing entry into this chamber has existed since the opening of this building to members of parliament and to the public generally. I may observe that there is a general entrance for the public in the centre, while there are other entrances for the employees of the House of Commons and of the Senate.

You misunderstand me, Mr. Speaker; I was not referring to any time during the actual sitting of the House. What I complain of is that at other times, in the morning for example, members are unable to come into the chamber to have access to their desks.
I know of no rule that prevents any hon. member from coming in by the side door.
There is only a small door in the rear of your chair, sir, by which we may enter the chamber.
Order.
Am I not in order, Mr. Speaker?
The hon. member may conclude his remarks.

What I am pointing out is that members cannot readily get access to their desks except when the House is sitting, and that is unreasonable. I wanted to come in this morning to get something out of my desk and the only means of access was a small door at the rear of your chair. That is not convenient either to members or to their friends, if they happen to have any with them; I do not see why it should be necessary to poke them through a back door.
Order.
I am informed that there is access to the House of Commons any day at any hour almost; the two side doors are open.
I .beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker, they are not open.
Order.
I pass through them myself every morning.

The House resumed, from March 24, consideration in committee of a proposed resolution with regard to the distribution of the canteen funds-Hon. Mr. Beland

Mr. Gordon in the chair.

There are two paragraphs particularly in the resolution which I desire to touch upon. The first is paragraph (2) which provides that the $100,000 shall be paid to a central board of three trustees appointed by the Governor in Council, without remuneration, to be used in such amounts and such manner-
As it may deem best for the maintenance and assisrt&nce of an adjustment service and bureau for the benefit of ex-service men and their dependents.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. May I ask
hon. members to desist from conversation? I am not able to hear the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) although I am within fifteen feet of him.

I can go a long way towards endorsing the principle embodied in that part

Canteen Funds
of the resolution. There are, however, some minor details to which I take exception, and I hope that the minister will amend the bill to conform with the suggestions I am going to make, which suggestions also conform in the main, I think, with the suggestions already made by various members from both sides of the House, indeed, by the minister himself. In the first place I notice the resolution does not provide that the three trustees shall be returned men. I understand the minister proposes that at least two shall be returned men. My suggestion is that all the trustees should come within this category. The only people interested in the fund are returned men, and therefore it should be handled exclusively by them, and there is no justification for the appointment of anyone other than a returned man as trustee.
Secondly, I suggest that if there is necessity for an adjustment bureau-and I am prepared to go so far as to admit that there is- then the money for its establishment should not be provided out of the canteen funds but out of public funds, and I quote the minister himself in support of my suggestion. Recently he laid on the table a return, No. 126, and1 on page 10, paragraph 13 of that return, Mr. Scammell, reporting to the minister on the question of the adjustment fund, said:
On my discussing the matter with you, however, you agreed with me and with the opinion expressed by Sir Arthur Currie after his interview with Mr. Oarruthers, referred to in his letter of May 7, to the Prime Minister, that while the continuance of the service given by the headquarters of the Great War Veterans' Association, or the Veterans' Alliance, Ottawa, pending the establishment, of an adjustment bureau, might be a proper charge against the disablement fund, it would also be a proper charge against public funds, and that this should, therefore, be handled in the form of a loan, and that you would make provision to reimburse the fund from a parliamentary appropriation. I advanced this money on May 16, 1923. Vote No. 543 was increased by $5,000 in order to provide for reimbursement. I received a cheque for $5,000 on August 25, 1923.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the minister has already recognized that the adjustment bureau is a proper charge cm public funds. In fact on one occasion he secured a vote from this House for $5,000 towards that very adjustment service that he now proposes to constitute to be financed by the canteen funds.

How much will it
cost?

It is very difficult to give
an exact estimate. In order to ascertain how much such service would cost, and to what extent it is necessary, I submit that the bureau must be independent of all soldier organizations and of the government itself. The work
of the bureau must be carried on at the discretion of the trustees, and I submit that the minister's suggestion to employ a representative of each of the soldier organizations in the service of the bureau is wrong in principle. By following this course we will get neither economy nor efficiency in the management of the $100,000. I suggest that an independent board of trustees will be best able to investigate and determine the exact number of employees required to provide this adjustment service. The board of trustees would employ men independent of the government and of the soldier organizations. That is why I suggested yesterday that in addition to Sir Arthur Currie a second member of the board of trustees should be selected by the major soldier organizations. For instance, there is in existence now, although it has been challenged by several members, an organization known as the Dominion Veterans' Alliance. Now, if there is a council representing the seven major soldier organizations, the council of the Dominion Veterans' Alliance, it can nominate a second trustee, and those two Can choose a third. When the board is constituted it will be in a position to employ a secretary and such other staff as imay be necessary to give the adjustment service required. All soldier organizations would be entitled to use that adjustment bureau. I repeat, I think the minister's suggestion that the staff of the bureau be composed of seven employees, one from each of the soldier organizations, is unsound. Furthermore, if such a suggestion be carried into effect, the trustees will have no discretion and no authority in the matter, because everything is provided for by the government before they take office.
Now, the necessity of such a board of trustees being independent both of the government and of the soldier organizations is well illustrated by the order in council which was under discussion some days ago, P.C. 1596. It refers to the disablement fund, and recites that:
This fund is being used generally for the purpose of small loans to pensioners and others who are in need of immediate assistance and who, in the opinion of the departmental investigations, would benefit by such assistance. The Dominion Veterans' Alliance, which represents the various veterans' organizations throughout Canada, has for a considerable time past maintained a service bureau in Ottawa for the purpose of assisting former members of the forces in the presentation of claims in respect of pension, medical treatment and other matters.
It was intended to utilize the Dominion Veterans' Alliance as the adjustment bureau under the provisions of the bill passed last year, as recited in this order in council. I
Canteen Funds

presume that the minister has since abandoned any thought of so using the Dominion Veterans' Alliance. Certain complications have arisen since that order in council was passed, which, I presume, will prohibit the utilization of the Dominion Veterans' Alliance or the G.W.V.A. As the minister has stated, the various soldier organizations other than the Great War Veterans' Association have objected to the providing of this adjustment service by any one organization. I think that objection is well founded; and it bears out my argument that the board of trustees should be independent both of the government and of the soldier organizations so that service can be given to all and each organization dealt with fairly and on an equal basis.
I would just like to reiterate the objections I have offered, and to express the wish that some of these suggestions may be embodied in -the bill: First, that the $100,000 be provided from the public funds; second, that the three trustees be all returned men; third, that they be appointed independently of the Governor in Council and in the manner suggested by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River and others.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not quite remember the suggestion that was made with regard to the appointment. Will my hon. friend recite that?

The suggestion was that Sir Arthur Currie be one trustee and that the second trustee be chosen by the -major soldier organizations. I suggested the Dominion Veterans' Alliance, if it is still in existence. If the council of that organization can get together and be truly representative of the seven soldier organizations I would be satisfied that a second trustee be selected by them.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Unanimously, or by a
majority?

The majority, I should think. I am quite sure the council would soon agree on a man. Then, the two thus appointed could choose a third, and failing agreement, the Governor in Council should be resorted to respecting the third appointee.
There is one other very vital paragraph in this resolution which has not been debated at all, and that is -paragraph 5, which provides that the balance of the canteen fund, consisting of about $2,000,000, shall be divided among the various provinces. It says:
The provincial allotments to be ipaid to a provincial board of trustees, appointed by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council in each province, without remuneration, empowered to receive and hold the provincial allotment and to ascertain the wishes of those interested and residing in the province concerning the

disposition of such allotment and to determine the object to which the allotment should be devoted, and to administer the same for such object or to provide for such administration by othens, and to do such other things as may be indicated in the order in council appointing them. The expenses in connection with the trust to be a charge on the allotment.
In the first place I object to these allotments going into the provinces without the purposes for which the moneys are to be used being specifically stated. The Ralston commission investigated this matter and they made certain general recommendations as to the purposes to which the money might well be devoted. This resolution does not suggest that any specific recommendations made by the Ralston commission, or any recommendations at all, for that matter should be adopted. It leaves it to a board of trustees, without remuneration, to ascertain the wishes of the returned men. But what chance would a board have in a large province of ascertaining the wishes of the returned men as a body, when seven years have elasped since the men were last interested in the fund? It would be utterly impossible for the board to find out the wishes of the men at this stage. We have, however, sufficient evidence before us to suggest certain specific purposes to which the board of trustees in the various provinces might devote these moneys, and I will enumerate some of them in a few minutes.
I offer the same objection to the appointment of the provincial boards of trustees by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council in each province that I urged to the appointment of the central board by the federal authorities. It is true that we cannot name one man who will be -acceptable to all in each province, but we know that in each province there are soldier organizations, represented by provincial units, and these might get together and agree upon one trustee. There are also in each of these provinces-and this is something which I think has been overlooked-the actual units that formed the Canadian corps in France.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Are they still maintained?

Still maintained, yes. I
doubt whether there is any unit of the Canadian corps which served in France that is not in existence to-day in the defence force of Canada. In most instances they are commanded by men who either commanded the units in the field or were high up in those units. In each of those units you will find a large sprinkling of officers, non-commissioned officers and men who actually served in those very units in the Canadian expeditionary force. In addition to that there is in each of these units a reserve battalion in which many men

Canteen Funds
who served in the corps are enlisted. They do not belong to the active militia, it is true, but they belong to the reserve and they are interested in this fund, although they may not be associated with the various returned soldier organizations. In addition, these units have their clubs and their regimental institutes. For instance, I could not give the exact number of members in my own unit, but I do know that on April 9 of each year between three and four hundred of these men turn out to a dinner. If that is true of all the units throughout the country you will readily see that a very large percentage of the men of the Canadian corps are still identified with the units of that corps.
Now what I suggest in the provincial administration of this fund is that the units which served in the Canadian corps might very well be given the privilege of appointing one of these trustees. There would be no difficulty about getting them to agree on a nominee because the units in British Columbia, for instance, and it is the same in Ontario, are brigaded, and the wishes of each unit could be ascertained by the brigade commander, and parsed on to the district commander. The same could be done in Ontario, where I believe the minister provides for the appointment of five trustees. There are, I believe, three military districts in Ontario. I do not know whether it is necessary to limit the number of these trustees to three in each province, or to five in Ontario; it might be well to have more than three. However, I have no serious Objection on that score. I appeal to the minister to consider this because I believe it will react for the benefit of all of us who are engaged in public life to-day. It will clear us completely. It works both ways, because there are in the various provinces administrations of both parties in this House, and if we adopt this suggestion it will clear our skirts absolutely of any suggestion that any political influence is being brought to bear in any of these appointments. I think the result would be for the greater good of the returned men as a whole.
I would also suggest that in the bill the minister cite the purposes to which the fund in the various provinces might be devoted.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
That was done to a limited extent in the bill of last year, in the last clause, which is reproduced in the bill that is going to follow this year. I do not know whether my hon. friend remembers that clause, but it reads as follows, and I think it carries out to a certain degree the ideas which he is now advancing. It says:
Without limiting the -powers conferred on the lieutenant governors in council the following general principles shall govern any distribution or apportionment of the amounts allotted to the said provincial boards of trustees:-
Then follow the recommendations:
(a)	Any plans formulated should be based on the assumption that there will be prospective beneficiaries for several years to come.
In other words, this recommendation precludes the immediate capital distribution of the fund amongst men. Then follows:
(b)	Any use of the fund for relief purposes should be limited to the class of case for which no relief is then available from governmental sources, and in particular to specially meritorious cases;
(c)	If the provision of scholarships in schools and universities is undertaken for specially promising children of ex-mem)bers of the forces or of members of the forces who have died, this should not necessarily be confined to the higher grades.
These are the only limitations. There are some limitations placed upon the lieutenant governors in council. I do not know to what extent these recommendations accord with what my hon. friend has in mind, but I just wanted to bring these facts to his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Not in council?

No. It is an incorporated
body. It is quite different from the -present proposaJ. This is a corporation, and the
Canteen Funds

corporation provides for the ap-4 p.m. pointment of a chairman by His Majesty the King. That may be in council; in all probability it is. The first chairman appointed was His Excellency the present Governor Generali of Canada, who has since been succeeded by Field Marshal Earl Haig. To continue:
Under the charter the governing body is a council of management consisting of a chairman, nominated by His Majesty the King, and twelve members, of whom nine are nominated by the British Legion, and the remaining three by the chairman to represent the ex-service men who do not belong to the British Legion. The present chairman of the council of management is Field Marshal Earl Haig. The first chairman was the present Governor General of Canada.
It will be noted that the British government has nothing whatever to do with the disposal of the fund. The council of management meet periodically and decide all questions of principle that arise, and supervise generally the work that is being done.
Then there is a memorandum as to the Administration committee and the Advisory Finance committee and their special agents:
The money is distributed principally under the following schemes:
And these are the schemes I commend to the minister, and whioh I suggest might be embodied in his bill:
Sick ex-service men scheme.
Removal grants for ex-service men.
Care of children not provided for by one or other of the fund's schemes.
Clearing homes for children who could not be properly cared for in their own homes owing to the death of one or both of their parents, and for children living in undesirable surroundings.
Parental care in cases where it is deemed undesirable that the children should remain in the care of their parents, relatives or guardians, notably in the case of very young children, and where the financial circumstances of the family make impossible the provision of adequate food and clothing for the children.
Then under the heading of convalescent treatment:
It is frequently the case that the parents of children recovering from illnesses are prevented by their straitened circumstances from arranging for the allnecessary convalescent treatment.
Special medical treatment for those needing special medical or dental treatment.
Surgical tuberculosis which is responsible for terrible deformities in thousands of unfortunate children.
After care-by which it is hoped to afford every child an opportunity of becoming a useful member of the community.
Apprenticeships and special training for children under 16 years of age form part of the scheme.
Then there is a memorandum on an educational scheme. They do not approve of the institution of any special scholarships as it was considered that a sufficient number already existed, or could be created by the Board of Education to cover the cases of the children whose abilities warranted them, I think these
IMr. Clark.]
are the main purposes to which the British fund is devoted, and purposes to which our fund might well be devoted, certainly in part.

Do the regulations which my hon. friend has just read form part of the trust, or were those regulations made by the trust itself after the trust was formed? I think these are only regulations. These were not embodied in the bill. I think they left it to their own trustees to make their own regulations.
It was not a bill at all in England. It was an incorporation.

Incorporated by
parliament, and I doubt very much if, in the letters patent, you would find all the details you have read. I think these details were arranged afterwards by the trustees.
That is quite possible.
That is what the minister proposes to do here.

But we are in a different position from that in which they were in England. They dealt with the matter expeditiously. These trustees in England have been in existence for quite a number of years, and we have the opportunity of profiting by their experience and eliminating such features as did not work, incorporating only the desirable features in our bill.

That is exactly
where I think my hon. friend makes a mistake. I think the bill should be as broad as possible, and I think the trustees should be left to make their own regulations.

That may be a matter of opinion, but a difficulty will confront these trustees in the various provinces from the fact that they will not be appointed until nearly seven years after the war is ended. Is that not right?
Quite right, but that does not matter.

We have had two governments in power with an opportunity of studying the situation, and in all these years no scheme has been devised defining any purpose to which this fund might properly be devoted. When two governments have failed to devise a scheme which is approved by all, how can we expect three poor trustees, without any remuneration, probably living hundreds of miles apart, to devise suitable schemes for the administration and disposal of the fund?

Canteen Funds
But my hon. friend thinks this could be done in the House of Commons?
I do.
I doubt it.

That is what I am suggesting. I am now suggesting a method whereby these trustees might be appointed, and leave this parliament free from all possible suspicion of bringing influence to bear upon them as to the purposes for which they might use the funds. I want it to be broad.

I am afraid your
first suggestion with regard to the hundred thousand dollars to be voted by this parliament would defeat entirely the object you have in view. If parliament votes a hundred thousand dollars, those who administer that fund will in the ordinary course be appointed by the Civil Service Commission.
No.

If the money is
voted by parliament the staff will have to be appointed by the Civil Service Commission.
The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment was not appointed by that commission.

But this will be a
special case.

I am not discussing the
hundred thousand dollars at this moment.
But you did.

Yes. My suggestion is that the three independent trustees be empowered by the bill to select and employ independently of parliament or the Civil Service Commission such persons as they see fit.
To come back to paragraph 5, I am suggesting similarly that trustees who are quite independent should be appointed; with general directions as to the purposes to which they may devote this fund. I think the position is so well expressed in a letter I received from a brother soldier that I might read a few words from the letter to show his opinion of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: A brother general or a brother soldier?

A brother soldier; it could
be both. He says:
If, after six years this is the best suggestion the government can make for the disposal of the canteen funds, bearing in mind the expert staff which it has had at its disposal, what could you and two other trustees do to make a plan to dispose of the money
that would be handed over to you with no expert staff at your disposal and with no remuneration for the time you would have to spend. Furthermore, if you were a trustee you would have out of work returned men sitting on your doorstep every night. You would be accused of favouritism, lack' of sympathy, embezzlement and God knows what before you finish.
There are other very appropriate remarks in that letter, but I feel quite convinced that that will be the situation if we simply pass the fund to trustees in the various provinces and ask them to devise a scheme, when we have men here who have studied the problem and can give them broad suggestions which could be contained in the bill, some of which they might follow and some of which they might reject. We can make the suggestions broad enough so as to avoid the possibility of manipulation of this fund, because certainly from the time the trustees are appointed they will be the target of manipulators. Let us safeguard the trustees and safeguard the fund in the interests of returned men. That is my sole object and I ask the minister to take it under consideration. He can rest assured that he will have the hearty co-operation not only of myself but of all other returned members who are interested in the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
kindly elaborate the method he has suggested for the appointment of the trustees in the different provinces? Do I understand him to contend that the Lieutenant Governor in Council in each province should not be the party to make the appointment in the first instance? If that is so, if the Lieutenant Governor in Council should not make the appointment, who should make the appointment of the trustees? Also in the third place, amongst What classes should the trustees be selected in order to carry out the object which he has in view?
From what classes?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
From what classes, whether
of soldiers or civilians or organized bodies of some kind; in other words from where should the trustees be brought that would constitute the board which would come up to the expectations of my hon. friend?

From what class? I say
unhesitatingly, only one class-the returned soldiers. I feel quite sure that I could name three trustees who would be acceptable to the returned soldiers generally in British Columbia, and I could draw them all from my hon. friend's party or from my own, for that matter. That is not the point. The recommendations should come from the returned soldiers' institutions. The units of the Cana-
Canteen Funds

dian corps now in existence in each province might well select one of the trustees. The various soldiers' organizations in each province might well select one of the trustees. That would be two, and the third might be selected by these two, or, failing that, by the Lieutenant Governor in Council. Another scheme might be that the Lieutenant Governor in Council might name the chairman, and the chairman accept the recommendation of the various returned soldiers' organizations for one trustee and the recommendation of the units of the Canadian corps in the province for the other trustee. For instance, if by any possible chance-and I do not think there will be such a chance-the units of the Canadian corps could not agree on one man and there were two men equally well thought of by those units, then if those two recommendations were handed in to the chairman, I would be quite satisfied th'at he should choose one trustee from these two or from >a number of recommendations. The matter would be very simple. In England that policy was followed out. Only one of twelve was named by the government. My memorandum says "By His Majesty the King," which I presume, as the minister suggests, means His Majesty the King in Council. If one is named by the Lieutenant Governor in Council, it will be quite satisfactory, as is done in England, to have the others named by the soldier's organizations or by the units of the Canadian corps in each province. That was done in England to the extent of twelve trustees.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I do not know whether I have exactly understood my hon. friend. If I have grasped the meaning of his remarks with reference to the appointment of provincial boards, they would tend to convey the following idea. Let us take Ontario as an illustration. The Lieutenant Governor of Ontario in Council would ask the different units in Ontario to nominate a candidate, then the different soldiers' organizations to name another candidate, and then the Lieutenant Governor in Council would appoint these two men and the chairman. Since we deal with Ontario as an illustration, we must not lose sight of the fact that in that province it was intended to have five trustees, on account of the size of the province,-the large number of returned men who have enlisted from or been discharged in that province, and the large number of pensioners there. Would my hon. friend be agreeable to something along this line-that the different militia units still in existence in Ontario would nominate two candidates, the returned soldiers' organizations nominate two, and the Lieutenant Governor

in Council appoint a chairman, a man naturally of outstanding reputation. Would that meet my hon. friend's views. As regards the other provinces, the suggestion is that the same method should be resorted to, that the units still in existence would recommend one candidate, the soldiers' organizations another and the Lieutenant Governor in Council appoint the chairman. This I think, is quite acceptable. I do not say at the present time that I accept the suggestion, but it is certainly worthy of consideration.
May I offer the suggestion that all the trustees should be returned men?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I would not say that. I did not say that.

I am aware that the
minister did not, but I want to be sure whether that is in his mind. I would suggest to the earnest consideration of the minister that all these trustees be returned men. There is a sufficiently large field to choose from and it seems a natural course to place this in the hands of returned men. There seems to be no cause for going outside of them, and I think it would be a source of satisfaction to the returned men to have the appointments made in this way.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
On general grounds I have no objection to the suggestion as it is made, but the recommendation was that the majority of each board should be made up of returned men. I have in mind, for instance, the case of the appointment of the royal commission. It was left open to the Governor in Council to appoint two returned men only and one civilian, but three returned men were appointed. I would submit the fact that an outstanding citizen, who would otherwise appear acceptable to the community at large as being eminently qualified for the position, should not be debarred because he did not happen to serve in the army, probably on account of his being disqualified by his age. A man of sixty or sixty-five occupying an exalted position amongst his co-citizens might be desirable as a member of that board. For instance, let us suppose the man who would be at the head of the patriotic fund-I do not know who he is, even by name

should be a man of sixty-five, eminently qualified for such a position. The fact that he did not serve in the army should not debar him from any appointment of this kind since he has served in a humanitarian capacity for a number of years. Although on general principle I agree that all trustees should be selected from amongst the men

Canteen Funds
themselves, I do not think that the selection should be confined entirely to the body of returned soldiers. So -long as we adopt the principle that the majority of each board shall consist of returned men I think we should leave some room for selecting suitable outsiders.

There is no difficulty
about finding suitable men among the returned soldiers themselves; capable men I have no doubt could be found both within and without the soldier body. But as >t!he fund is the property of the returned men it seems to me only proper and rational to band over the administration, of it to those who are directly and more particularly -concerned. Undoubtedly all of us desire to do our utmost to satisfy -the returned soldiers, and my interpretation of th-eir feelings is that they wish to have the opportunity of administering their own funds rather than having someone assist them, however well qualified that assistant might be. Men can be found, I say, within the ranks of those who have been overseas who would be perfectly capable of handling -the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The trustees will have to
serve without remuneration under this legislation, and that provision in itself might be an obstacle in the way of some returned men who might on all other grounds be excellent members of -the hoard. Some returned men might not be favoured with worldly things, and although they might be thoroughly qualified for the position they might find it impossible to serve without remuneration, losing probably a few days in the month. That .is what I have in mind at the moment. My suggestion is that we do not bind the hands either of the federal government or of the provinces in the selection of the trustees. If it were found that some man might make an acceptable -trustee, perfectly satisfactory to the returned men themselves, it would be unfortunate if some provision in the statute precluded his appointment. Since this resolution has been before the House one man has been suggested to me as -acceptable to the returned men; I do not propose to give his name, but I have every reason, to believe that he would be satisfactory. I do not think he would serve on the central board of trustees, although he might be asked -to serve in Toronto; butt I am quite sure that he would be an ideal man, quite acceptable to all ex-service men. If we provide in the statute that no man shall be appointed who has not been overseas we are going to tie the
hands of those who may make the appointments. and in that way it seems to me we shall seriously handicap them. Generally speaking, the principle suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. MacLaren) is a good one, and one to which I subscribe myself. I should be sorry, however, to see the law so framed as to make it impossible for some outstanding man, who might do splendid service on the board, to be appointed merely because through age or ill health he had been unable to join the forces. That is the point I have in mind.

I can see no reason why
the amount allotted to each province should be hedged around with conditions of any kind. The minister knows as well as I do that we have had the fund under our care for a number of years and we have had representations from all quarters as to its disposal. A committee on soldiers' civil re-establishment has dealt with it more or less exhaustively for years and no decision has been arrived at; and it is now apparent that we are deciding to pass our responsibility over to the provinces.
I can see no reason at all why this should be done. The minister mentioned the province of Ontario by way of illustration and I may refer to the same province also. I have no reason to suppose that the members of the Ontario government, present or future, would have the soldiers' interests less at heart than the members of this parliament or of the present government, and I do not see, therefore, why, if we are to divide the fund in the manner suggested, we should not hand it over to the men in every way untrammelled. As a matter of fact, when the minister brings down his bill I would suggest that it be entitled, "a bill for the purpose of passing the buck". We are simply trying to shirk our responsibility and to pass it on to someone else, hedged around with all sorts of difficulties, and I can see no possible reason for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am afraid that if the
government decided to administer the fund the hon. member himself would object; he would want to know why we did not leave it to the provinces.

There is absolutely no
danger of hon. gentlemen taking that course; the government of which the minister is a member are so used to passing the buck that it is nothing new. I want to say a few words now regarding the $100,000. Let me point out that this canteen fund belongs to the rank and file of the Canadian army. I was not here yesterday while this question was being discussed, but as I said a few days ago, this
Canteen Funds

money belongs to the men entirely and I can see no possible reason why $100,000 or any sum at all should be taken from the fund for the purpose of creating a third or a fourth bureau at Ottawa. We must remember in the first place that the country undertook to place our returned wounded men in the same position relatively that they would have occupied had they not been wounded. And our pension officers are for that purpose. It is quite true that our pension board has been more or less a sell, and probably there is a good deal of reason in some cases; but to get over that difficulty we appointed another bureau, the Federal appeal board. And both of these institutions have been maintained at the public expense. Now it is necessary to have a third body to see that justice is done the returned men. Well, why not pay that body too? Why should this amount be abstracted from the canteen fund of the soldier himself? In the course of this debate I fancy most of us have wandered somewhat from the subject. This canteen fund does not belong to the dis-ab.ed man alone but equally to the man who returned A-l. Everyone on returning from overseas was supposed to be placed in the same position, as regards earning power, as he held before the war. I am absolutely opposed therefore to the abstraction of this amount from the fund, and this is the view taken by the majority of the returned men. It is also the view taken by Sir Arthur Currie as quoted yesterday, although I have not the extract before me. He distinctly stated that the amount necessary for this adjustment bureau should be taken from the public fund.

Mr. Chairman, in my opinion no condition should be laid down by this House in regard to the appointment of trustees. I would leave it in such a way that any representations would be considered by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council. As to the suggestion bjr the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) that military units now in existence should have representation, I am not in agreement with him. There may be military unite in Vancouver, but to-day throughout the interior of British Columbia there are practically none, and I am convinced that to lay down the condition that such military units should have representation would create dissatisfaction. I am sure every one in this House, and more especially the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, wishes to evolve a measure that will prove as near satisfactory to the returned men and to the country as is possible, but I do not think we are likely to reach this desirable 
result- if we attempt to lay down conditions regarding the appointment of trustees. Certainly I cannot subscribe to such a course and I cannot agree that military units now in existence should be given representation.

Would the hon. member deny to five hundred members of a military unit, all of -whom served in France, any voice in the disposal of this fund? Furthermore, will he say there are no military units in existence in the upper country of British Columbia?

I would not debar the five hundred men identified with a military unit from any voice in the disposal of this fund, I would allow their representations to be considered to the fullest possible extent. But I contend that the representation of military units now in existence is a minor consideration, for these men are sure to be connected in some way with the different soldiers' organizations, through whom they can express their views.

I would wager that not one in fifty of the five hundred men I have referred to belong to any soldier organization. How many ipaid-up subscriptions does the hon. member think all the soldier organizations have to-day?
I should not like to get into any controversy over soldier organizations.
You are suggesting that they ought to belong to the soldier organizations if they are to have a voice in the disposal of these funds.

No. I want to see them have representation, but I think the administration of this money should not have any military aspect whatever. I believe I am safe in saying that a very high percentage of the returned men want to keep the fund free from military interference. The hon. member for Burrard would apparently bring the administration back to a war status. Replying to his second question, there are very few military units throughout the interior of British Columbia. So far as my knowledge goes, there is only a small nucleus of a military formation at Kamloops.
How about the B.C. Horse?
Where throughout the interior does it exist?

I am asking my hon. friend the question. It is in his neighbourhood.

Canteen Funds

West Kootenay is not anywhere near my neighbourhood. At one time there was a formation of the B.C. Horse, but we have no military units of that nature now. The consensus of opinion is that the time is not opportune for a military unit. But that is getting away from the question before the committee. I do not want to be identified with the laying down of certain conditions regarding the appointment of these trustees and the administration of the fund. I have the fullest trust that any outstanding man, whether he is connected with a military unit, a soldier organization or any other concern, will give his best efforts to the administration of this fund in the interests of the returned men and the country. I believe if we keep away from the laying down of the conditions to which I have referred it will be better not only for the returned men but for the country.

I do not wish to delay the resolution, but I desire to make a few points and to emphasize those I made yesterday, because we intend to keep faith with the minister that the resolution shall be permitted to go through before six o'clock. I think before the minister brings in the bill based on the resolution he should bear in mind the suggestions made from different parts of the House. I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Humphrey). He appears to think that we should not be discussing this resolution at all. But surely the time to discuss a resolution or a bill is before it is passed.

I do not wish to be misunderstood by my hon. friend. I did not imply that we should not discuss the resolution at all, I merely said that we should not lay down conditions respecting the appointment of the. trustees and the administration of the fund.

It is better to lay down
conditions before the resolution passes than to complain about them afterwards. My hon. friend said that the minister especially is anxious to get this matter arranged properly for the benefit of the returned men; but while giving him credit for this, I think we may take it for granted that we are all anxious to bring about a result wholly satisfactory to those concerned. There are two or three points I wish to make in regard to the $100,000 from the canteen fund. I dealt with this phase of the subject yesterday and was supported by the hon. member for Burrard, the member for Parry Sound and some others. The view we take is that this $100,000 should not be
taken from the canteen fund and that the expenses of the adjustment bureau should be provided for by an estimate passed in this House, the appropriation to be handled entirely by the central board of trustees, independently of any department of the government. I am on solid ground in taking that attitude. It is the view not only of practically all members who have spoken, but also of Sir Arthur Currie, as the hon. member for Parry Sound pointed out a few moments ago. The hon. member did not have Sir Arthur Currie's comments on the subject before him, but I have them here and I would like to quote from some statements Sir Arthur Currie has made in this connection. I do this because if the minister agrees with what we are proposing I would like to see him arrange his bill so that we can avoid amendments afterwards. Sir Arthur Currie, writing to the Prime Minister in May, 1923, speaking' of an adjustment bureau, says:
1 ain firmly convinced that such an organization is desirable and necessary and Mr. MacNeil informs me that the Hon. Dr. Beland and yourself hold similar views. I believe myself that such a service is a proper charge upon government funds and its maintenance could be justified to the members of the House.	.
Then in another letter under date of May 19, a few days later, addressed to the Minister of Soldiere' Civil Re-establishment, he says:
Such action I hold to have been illegal-
That is, the use of money from the canteen fund or the disablement fund for other purposes.
The canteen	funds are funds	in which	all	thesoldiers have an	interest and they	are trust funds	andneither the government nor any	department	of	the
government has any mandate to expropriate one cent of those funds.
In another letter dated November 27th, 1924, he says to the minister:
I am more than ever convinced that this service must be kept going and I take it the government has admitted the principle by its appointment of a soldiers' adviser in the	large centres of	population	in	the
Dominion. There can be no question in the minds of all right thinking people that the adjustment service as carried on by the headquarters of the G.W.V.A. is urgently necessary and must not be allowed tc lapse. You know that my opinion is that the cost of this service should be borne by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Would my hon. friend read further on?

I just quoted the words
applicable to my remarks. That is the reason I stopped.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I think he says something about taking such an adjustment bureau away from the control of the government.
Canteen Funds

Of course; he has said
that a number of times. I think we all agree, the minister himself included, that that should be done. I continue the reading of the paragraph:
I believe that you are willing to bear this cost but that you cannot agree with the G.W.V.A. as to the organization which should be provided for that service.
No, he does not refer to it in that letter, but he may in some other letters. I quoted an opinion of his yesterday that the bureau should be independent of any branch of the government. I quote further from the same letter:
You know my views regarding the use of any part of the canteen fund or the disablement fund for this purpose.
That is, the purpose of an adjustment bureau.
I regSrd both funds as trust funds and I think that any disposal which has already been made, while perhaps justifiable, was not in accordance with the spirit of a trust.
I think these are sufficient quotations to show the attitude Sir Arthur Currie takes in the matter. Now, here is the statement of a prominent war veterans' organization as sent to a member of this House-to the leader of the opposition, as a matter of fact -from Toronto on March 6th, nineteen days ago. Mr. J. H. Davidson, President of the Riverdale Command, Great War Veterans' Association of Canada, says:
Sir,-The Command of the G.W.V.A. of which I have the honour to be the president most strenuously oppose the payment out of the canteen funds of any moneys to any association, the Great War Veterans' Association included. We maintain, sir, that no association of ex-service men no matter how strong in membership it may be has no right to receive from the canteen funds any moneys whatsoever.
He really contradicts himself there, but it is simply an inadvertence in the wording. A little further on he says-

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
May I ask who writes
that?
I gave the name a moment ago-J. H. Davidson, President o-f the River-dale Command, Great War Veterans' Association. I am just giving it as an outside opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That association has already received funds from the canteen fund?

It is possible; I cannot
help that. I am simply quoting his opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Does this gentleman say
that should not be done?
Yes, he apparently opposes it very strenuously.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
He was assuredly, then,
not a member of the Great War Veterans' Association when that association received large amounts of money from the canteen funds, appropriated by a former government.

Well, he is opposing it, anyway. Apparently he opposes any moves that were made to convey moneys of the canteen fund to the Great War Veterans' Association or any other organization. He says:
We maintain, sir, that no association of ex-service men, no matter how strong in membership it may be, has the right to receive from the canteen funds any moneys whatsoever.
Then, a little further down:
If the bill, when introduced, or rather when it is voted upon next time, makes no reference to the payment of any moneys to the Veterans' Alliance or to any other service organization, but that it simply allocates the balance of the canteen funds now in the hands of the Receiver-General to the different provinces in the proportion as suggested last year, that is so much to each of the different provinces and the sums to the Red Cross of TJ.S.A. and Great Britain, this will be in line with our views. We feel that if at this time it is necessary for moneys to he available for the veterans to have a service bureau to assist them to prosecute their claims for pensions, adjustments, etc., it is the duty of the government of the day to set aside by parliamentary procedure the necessary moneys, and not that the returned men shall be called upon to furnish them from out of the small amount they were fortunate enought to accumulate whilst overseas by their purchase (out of their pay) in different canteens.
This geutleman represents a prominent organization of war veterans, and that is his opinion. So I think the minister should seriously consider the introduction into the bill of a clause which would permit the adjustment bureau to be handled not out of the canteen funds but out of the moneys of the people of Canada and by trustees independent of any branch of the government or of the opposition. That is the first point. Then, in regard to the trustees, this point has been dealt with also; I dealt with it yesterday myself and others have referred to it. I hope the minister will live up to what I think he agreed to yesterday in regard to arranging the appointment oif the central trustees-and if he can carry it to the extent of arranging similarly the appointment of the provincial trustees I will follow -him- namely, that no strings should be attached to them, politically or otherwise. In other words, if possible one trustee should be selected by this parliament, and one by the different returned soldiers' organizations combined, and then let these two choose a third.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend would not
allow the Governor in Council to appoint one?

Canteen Funds

If these two could not
agree, I would say the Governor in Council should appoint a third member. But I do not see why the government should be particularly anxious to appoint one. It is not government money.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
If the government is to
be distrusted as much as that, I wonder why the fund was placed in its hands.

There was nowhere else
to place it, as far as I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
It could be put in a
thousand other places. It could be deposited with a bank or trust company, for instance.
As a matter of fact somebody suggests that it was another government in whose hands the money was placed. However, I was not going to refer to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
And they dealt with the
funds very poorly.

I do not agree with the
minister; and I am willing to debate that point with him if he wants to take the time to do it. I think we dealt with them very honestly and fairly. Whatever distributions were made were in proportion to the numbers in the different organizations. As far as distrust is concerned, I think the minister is simply importing that into the discussion. It is* not a case of distrust, it is simply a case of endeavouring to get these trustees appointed in such a way that they will be outside of politics altogether. This money does not belong to the government .or to parliament; it belongs to the returned men entirely, and I think the returned men should handle it. It should not be handled in any way by this government or any other-I happen to speak of this government because this is the government which is arranging to distribute the funds. I am not making this suggestion because of any distrust, but because I think the trustees should be absolutely above anything in the shape of political influence. I have no doubt the minister could mention many names to the House that would absolutely satisfy me. I am not suggesting that the trustees should be Conservatives or anything of that sort. I have heard a number of names mentioned already, among them the name of Sir Arthur Currie, who I believe is a Liberal. Another very prominent man in this city I heard mentioned jmsterday. He is an outstanding Liberal, and his brother is an exceptionally outstanding Liberal, and if this man was appointed he would certainly be satisfactory to
me. So I am not thinking of the political side of it at all. My only desire is that so far as possible the trustees shall be appointed in such a way that they will be outside of politics altogether. If this money belonged to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment that would be a different proposition. Then the government themselves should appoint the trustees. But this is money that belongs to the returned -men, and I do not see any reason why the government should wish to appoint the trustees; I think they should welcome the opportunity to get rid of all responsibility in the matter.
In regard to the trustees, I rather lean to the idea of their being returned men, not because I have not the same respect as the minister has for many men who did not go overseas, particularly those who were too old to go. I know very many men who did not join the forces, and who never did anything directly in a military way, yet who are perhaps equally deserving with the men who went overseas. I would be the last to suggest any distrust of anybody who did not go overseas simply on that account. At the same time, I believe you would get more satisfaction among the returned men if this fund were handled by the returned men entirely; that is the only reason, I have for making this suggestion. Otherwise, I should not care to put up a fight on the matter at all. I think the government would be wise, when they bring in the bill, to provide for returned men entirely handling the funds, especially in view of the fact that we have four or five hundred thousand returned men in the country; and though, of course, there are many able men outside the ranks of those who went overseas, certainly among four or five hundred thousand men you could get just as outstanding men as you would find outside. I think it is only a fair proposition, therefore, that this money, which belongs entirely to the men who served overseas, should! be handled entirely by the returned men themselves.
There is one other point, and that is in regard to the passing of the resolution. There are some others who wish to speak, I presume, but I wish to point out this: Last evening we had a little bit of discussion about carrying this resolution over until this afternoon, and my good friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) argued that the principle of the resolution did not deal with the details. Perhaps he was right. At the same time, if by passing the resolution we are agreeing to the principle that there is to !be a distribution
Canteen Funds

of the can*teen funds, though I may be quite agreeable to that, I do not wish it to be understood that we will not move amendments if the government does not introduce some that have been suggested; for example, along the line of the allotment of the $100,000. I want it to be understood that when the resolution is presented, we are at liberty to move any amendments we think desirable to be made in the bill. I presume that is understood by the minister.
There is one other point, and that is the point made by my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark) regarding the putting of limitations on the trustees. I notice 5 p.m. that clause 10 of the bill of last year, Bill No. 253, as passed by the House of Commons on the 16th of July, of last year, provides:
(a)	Any plans formulated should be based on the assumption that there will be prospective beneficiaries for several years to come;
(b)	Any use of the fund for relief purposes should be limited to the class of case for which no relief is then available from governmental sources, and in particular to specially meritorious cases;
(c)	If the provision of scholarships in schools and universities is undertaken for specially promising children of ex-members of the forces or of members of the forces who have died, this should not necessarily be confined to the higher grades.
Of course, I know these subclauses are put in partly conditional 'upon, 'their adoption. At the same time, the fact remains that in last year's bill the government did introduce some limitations as to the manner in which these fund^ should !be used by the different provinces, and if there are some good suggestions for us in the uses to which the funds in Great Britain have been put, which were cited by my hon. friend from Burrard-and I think some of the suggestions were good-there is no reason in the world why one or two subclauses might not be added to the bill of last year. I have not seen the bill of this year, and I do not know whether it contains these subclauses.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.

There is no reason, to my mind, why the minister could not add another subclause, or more, exactly on the same lines as this, to provide that the funds shall be used entirely for the benefit of the returned men and their dependents in the different provinces.

Suppose those
restricting clauses are embodied in the bill who is going to prepare the further regulations that will be needed both for the provincial boards and the central board? Will the central board prepare them?
They were incorporated in the bill of last year. Perhaps the minister could answer that.

What were incorporated in the bill of last year were the restrictions my hon. friend has mentioned. They were not what I might call absolute regulations to guide the provincial boards as well as the central board. The central board, in my opinion, should be the body that will provide the further regulations that will be needed either for the central board itself or for the provincial boards.
May I go a little bit further and suggest that the main body to be organized under this resolution is the central board. And the very fact that my hon. friend has mentioned Sir Arthur Currie's name as chairman of this board, is proof that this board is considered the most important board that will be appointed under this resolution. So why not leave to the central board the work of ascertaining from the different associations of returned men 'in the different provinces what men they would choose to sit on this board of appeal for each province? That is the proper body, in my opinion, to consult with the associations in the different provinces, and after consulting with them they could recommend to the Lieutenant Governor in Council of -each province the names of those who should be appointed to form these boards. I think that meets the opinion of everybody, and I think also it is a concrete, and practical proposal.
Mr, MANION: I would agree with that.
This discussion has gone on now for some four or five sittings-

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend allow m-e first to reply? I understand he is entering upon another subject.	.
My hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) has referred to the limitations in clause 10 which were incorporated in the bill of last year. I will deal with that in a moment. But before we go any further, I would like to explain to the committee that the central board, though it is so named, will have nothing to do at all with the provincial allotments.
I did not mean that, but in the bill you can give power to the central board to prepare the way before the other bodies are appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) has suggested that the central board should be given certain
